AGENTS.md

Source: AGENTS.md

Project purpose

This repository contains qgsim, a small R teaching package for quantitative genetics and breeding-simulation examples.

The package currently focuses on two ideas:

  1. Simulating simple multi-generational pedigrees.
  2. Demonstrating gene dropping from parental haplotypes using interchangeable R, C++, and Fortran implementations.

The package is intentionally small and educational. Do not describe it as a complete production breeding simulator.

Current exported functionality

The current main user-facing functions are:

  • simulate_pedigree()
  • gene_drop_generation()

simulate_pedigree()

simulate_pedigree() simulates a simple multi-generational pedigree.

It returns a data frame with:

  • id
  • sire
  • dam
  • generation
  • sex

Founder parents are represented by NA.

gene_drop_generation()

gene_drop_generation() simulates marker inheritance for one generation from parental haplotypes and a mating design.

It supports:

  • engine = "R"
  • engine = "C++"
  • engine = "Fortran"

The R code handles validation, random event generation, and the user-facing interface.

The C++ and Fortran code implement the deterministic marker-level inheritance loop.

For the same seed, the R, C++, and Fortran engines should produce identical outputs.

The implementation is a simple single-chromosome teaching example. It is not a full production gene-dropping simulator.

Repository type

This is an R package repository.

Typical content includes:

  • R/: R source code and wrappers
  • src/: C++/Fortran/C native code
  • tests/testthat/: package tests
  • man/: generated roxygen documentation
  • vignettes/: long-form tutorials and collaborator guides
  • docs/: generated pkgdown website output
  • README.md: package overview
  • DESCRIPTION: package metadata and dependencies
  • NAMESPACE: generated by roxygen2
  • qgsim.Rproj: RStudio project file

General rules

  • Work only inside this repository.
  • Do not commit changes unless explicitly asked.
  • Check git status --short before editing.
  • If the working tree is dirty, identify existing changes before editing.
  • Do not overwrite unrelated user changes.
  • Prefer small, reviewable edits.
  • Show the diff after edits.
  • Do not delete files unless explicitly asked.
  • Do not push to GitHub unless explicitly asked.
  • Do not create or modify remotes.

R package rules

  • Preserve valid R package structure.
  • Do not edit NAMESPACE or man/ by hand unless explicitly asked.
  • Use roxygen comments for documentation updates.
  • Run devtools::document() when roxygen documentation or exports change.
  • Keep exported API changes deliberate and documented.
  • Avoid adding new dependencies unless clearly justified.
  • If adding dependencies, update DESCRIPTION and explain why.
  • Prefer base R where practical.
  • Keep examples small and reproducible.

Native-code rules

The package now contains compiled-code examples under src/.

Native code currently supports the C++ and Fortran engines in gene_drop_generation().

When modifying native code:

  • Be conservative.
  • Keep the R, C++, and Fortran engines numerically consistent.
  • Do not generate random numbers inside C++ or Fortran.
  • Random events should be generated in R and passed to compiled code.
  • C++ and Fortran should implement deterministic marker-level inheritance loops.
  • Preserve native routine registration in src/init.c.
  • Do not change .Call() or .Fortran() interfaces without updating R wrappers and tests.
  • Do not add OpenMP or external shared-library machinery unless explicitly asked.
  • Do not commit generated native artifacts such as .o, .obj, .dll, .so, .dylib, .lib, or .exe.

Testing rules

Use the smallest relevant check for the change.

Common checks:

devtools::load_all()
devtools::test()

For focused tests:

testthat::test_file("tests/testthat/test-simulate-pedigree.R")
testthat::test_file("tests/testthat/test-gene-drop-generation.R")

For command-line checks:

Rscript -e "devtools::load_all(); testthat::test_dir('tests/testthat')"

For documentation changes:

devtools::document()

For package website changes:

pkgdown::build_site()

Ask before running long checks such as full R CMD check, unless explicitly requested.

Documentation rules

Use this convention:

  • README.md: short package overview and links
  • man/: generated function documentation
  • vignettes/: tutorial/article source files
  • docs/: generated pkgdown website output

Edit tutorial sources in vignettes/.

Do not edit generated files under docs/ manually.

When pkgdown documentation changes, rebuild the site with:

pkgdown::build_site()

Keep documentation aligned with implemented functionality.

Do not document old or removed APIs such as:

  • breeding_scheme()
  • qgsim_compile()
  • qgsim_run()
  • qgsim_result
  • backend registries

unless they are clearly described as removed or future ideas.

Scientific and modelling rules

  • Do not invent simulation results, benchmarking claims, or performance claims.
  • Do not describe qgsim as a complete breeding-scheme simulator.
  • State clearly when examples are simplified teaching examples.
  • simulate_pedigree() is a simple random pedigree simulation.
  • gene_drop_generation() is a simple single-chromosome gene-dropping implementation.
  • Avoid adding biological complexity without tests and clear documentation.
  • Keep terminology consistent: pedigree, sire, dam, generation, haplotype, genotype, map, recombination.

Git and generated-file rules

Before reporting back, check:

git status --short

Generated or local files that should not be committed include:

  • .Rproj.user/
  • .Rhistory
  • .RData
  • .Ruserdata
  • .quarto/
  • AGENTS.md
  • native build artifacts such as .o, .obj, .dll, .so, .dylib, .lib, .exe

If native build artifacts appear after devtools::load_all(), report them and ask before deleting unless the user explicitly requested cleanup.

Preferred response style

When reporting back:

  • State what was inspected.
  • State what was changed.
  • List checks run.
  • Mention checks not run.
  • Highlight risks or follow-up work.
  • Keep recommendations concrete and actionable.
